Volume 13 · Chapter 08

Information economics and screening

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v13-c07

By the endSolve screening and signaling models with participation and incentive constraints.

Volume 13 · Chapter 8

Information economics and screening

A seller who cannot observe a buyer’s willingness to pay may profit by withholding quality from some buyers. An informed worker may spend resources on education even when education adds nothing to productivity. Both problems involve private information, but the uninformed seller designs a committed menu in the first, while the informed worker chooses a signal and other agents interpret it in the second. The timing of commitment, observation and participation determines the relevant constraints.

Capability. Derive and solve finite and continuous screening problems, including exclusion and bunching; establish when random contracts add no value; characterize all pure equilibria in an explicit education model; and prove what a stated belief refinement selects, including a boundary where selection fails. Six original worked cases and twelve solved exercises distinguish incentive compatibility, participation, global optimality and empirical interpretation.

Prerequisites. Uncertainty and information supplies expected utility and convexity. Static games and refinements supplies best responses and equilibrium refinements. Dynamic and repeated games supplies contingent strategies, Bayes consistency and the importance of off-path beliefs. Integration and constrained concave optimization were developed in Volume 2. The present continuous-signal model is defined directly; its analysis does not follow from a finite-game sequential-equilibrium existence theorem.

Every distribution, quality, cost and wage below is an original instructional assumption. Utility and money are measured in compatible units; quality and education are nonnegative quantities. The cases establish implications of specified models, not estimated behavior or evidence that an actual market satisfies their assumptions.

1. A committed menu and the complete finite IC test

A seller faces one buyer with privately known value parameter θ in the finite ordered set θ1<⋯<θn. Each type has probability fi>0, with Σfi=1. A contract specifies quality q∈[0,Q] and payment t from buyer to seller, where 0<Q<∞. Buyer utility is θq−t; the outside option has quality and payment zero. Seller cost is c(q), with c continuous on [0,Q] and c(0)=0. The seller commits to its menu before the buyer chooses, quality is enforceable, and payments have no separate borrowing or limited-liability constraint. Later sections identify which conclusions require risk neutrality or convex cost.

Adverse selection is the difficulty created by private type before contracting. A higher θ values an increment of quality more: for q′>q, the utility difference θ(q′−q)−(t′−t) increases strictly in θ. This is the single-crossing property used here. It is a property of preferences, not a conclusion that every optimal contract supplies distinct qualities.

A direct menu assigns (qi,ti) to report i. Define truthful utility Ui=θiqi−ti. Weak incentive compatibility (IC) and individual rationality (IR) are

Ui≥θiqj−tj for every i,j;   Ui≥0 for every i.

Tie convention. When truth is a best report, we evaluate the outcome in which the buyer reports truthfully; when this gives zero utility, we allow the buyer to participate. An excluded type is assigned (0,0). These are explicit selections among best responses. Weak IC/IR does not promise unique implementation or participation under a different tie rule. In particular, a zero-rent buyer can choose the outside option, and a bunched pair may receive the same contract.

Single-buyer menu reduction, with proof. Consider any committed menu in this maintained class and a selected maximizing contract for each type, allowing the outside option. Label those selected contracts by type. A type’s assigned contract was at least as attractive as every contract selected by another type and at least as attractive as the outside option. The resulting direct menu is IC/IR and reproduces the selected quality, payment and seller payoff. Conversely, offer the contracts of an IC/IR direct menu: truthful selection and participation are best responses by definition. Thus optimizing over direct menus loses no selected outcome within this single-agent committed-menu class. This argument assumes the original selected maxima exist; it is not a general revelation theorem for multiple agents, renegotiation, unverifiable quality or additional private actions.

Finite characterization. Write Δθi=θi+1−θi>0. A quality/utility list is IC if and only if q is nondecreasing and

Δθiqi≤Ui+1−Ui≤Δθiqi+1,   i=1,…,n−1.

Necessity. For i<j, the two cross-report constraints give

(θj−θi)qi≤Uj−Ui≤(θj−θi)qj.

Since the type difference is positive, qi≤qj. Adjacent types give the displayed increment bounds. Sufficiency. For i<j, sum the adjacent lower bounds. Monotonicity gives Σk=ij−1Δθkqk≥(θj−θi)qi. Sum the upper bounds to obtain Uj−Ui≤ΣΔθkqk+1≤(θj−θi)qj. These are exactly both cross-report inequalities for every pair. Setting ti=θiqi−Ui completes the construction.

Minimal rents. For any nondecreasing q≥0, the seller can choose

U1=0,   Ui=Σk<iΔθkqk,   ti=θiqi−Ui.

The lower adjacent bounds bind; the upper bounds follow from monotonicity. Every Ui is nonnegative. Any other IC/IR list at the same q has U1≥0 and, by summing lower bounds, utility at least this amount for each type. Replacing it by the displayed list weakly raises each payment, so it weakly raises expected profit. Positive type probabilities make any strictly unnecessary rent costly. This is why low IR and downward adjacent IC can be imposed at an optimum. It does not say they are the only binding constraints: exclusion can make several rents zero, and bunching can bind further IC constraints.

Virtual-surplus identity. Define

φi=θi−(Δθi/fi)Σj>ifj for i<n;   φn=θn.

To keep the identity’s scope precise, write an arbitrary IC list as Ui=U1+Σk<iΔθkqk+di, where d1=0 and di≥0 by the lower bounds. Interchanging two finite sums gives

ΣifiUi=U1+Σk<nΔθkqkΣi>kfi+Σifidi,
Π=Σifi[φiqi−c(qi)]−U1−Σifidi.

At minimal rents U1=di=0, so optimize the first sum on 0≤q1≤⋯≤qn≤Q. Increasing low quality generates both direct revenue and additional rent for all higher types; φ includes that rent cost. Continuity on this compact set gives an optimum. If c is strictly convex, the weighted objective is strictly concave because every fi>0, so the optimal quality vector is unique. Minimal-rent payments are then uniquely determined within our selected direct representation. Individual first-order conditions solve the problem only when their proposed allocation is feasible and globally justified.

Worked case 1: three types, exclusion and zero rents

Take θ=(1,2,3), f=(1/2,1/4,1/4), Q=5 and c(q)=q²/2. The virtual values are (0,1,3). For any scalar φ, maximizing φq−q²/2 on [0,5] gives q=min(5,max(0,φ)): complete the square when φ≥0, and for φ<0 every positive q makes the value negative. Here the pointwise maximizers are already ordered. Consequently they maximize the sum over the smaller feasible monotone set globally.

The solution is q=(0,1,3), with U=(0,0,1) and t=(0,2,8). The matrix of truthful utility minus utility from each report, with true types as rows, is

((0,1,5),(0,0,2),(1,0,0)).

Every entry is nonnegative. The middle type is indifferent between participating and taking the excluded type’s contract; the high type is indifferent between its own contract and the middle contract. Our announced tie convention therefore matters. The positive quality of the middle type does not imply positive rent.

Profit is (1/4)(2−1/2)+(1/4)(8−9/2)=5/4. Expected buyer rent is 1/4. Total surplus, defined as expected θq−q²/2, is profit plus rent, 3/2; payments are transfers between buyer and seller. With observable types the surplus-maximizing q=θ is feasible and yields 15/8. The screening allocation therefore loses 3/8 of total surplus, even though it is optimal for the informed-menu seller.

Worked case 2: a nonregular distribution and an exact bunching certificate

Now use θ=(2,3,4), f=(1/2,1/10,2/5), Q=5, with the same cost. Virtual values are (1,−1,4). Unconstrained scalar optimization would give (1,0,4), violating monotonicity. Setting the first quality to one and the second to zero cannot be repaired by clever payments: the necessity part of the IC theorem rules it out.

Pool the first two qualities at x. Their contribution is (1/2)(x−x²/2)+(1/10)(−x−x²/2), whose unique maximizer is x=[(1/2)−(1/10)]/[(1/2)+(1/10)]=2/3. The candidate is q*=(2/3,2/3,4). A proof of global optimality must also cover allocations that do not pool. The gradient of the full concave objective at q* is g=(1/6,−1/6,0). For any feasible q, the exact quadratic expansion is

Π(q)−Π(q*)=g·(q−q*)−(1/2)Σifi(qi−q*i)²
=(q1−q2)/6−(1/2)Σifi(qi−q*i)²≤0.

Order gives the first inequality, and the strictly positive probabilities make equality possible only at q=q*. This proves a unique global allocation, rather than merely finding a stationary point on a guessed face. Minimal rents give U=(0,2/3,4/3) and t=(4/3,4/3,44/3). The first two contracts are identical. All IC gaps are ((0,0,20/3),(0,0,10/3),(0,0,0)); all rents are nonnegative. Profit is 10/3. This example proves one finite bunching solution; it is not a theorem that arbitrary decreasing intervals can always be averaged without checking their neighboring constraints.

The inspected Holmström slides, 19–23 develop a procurement version. Their transfers run principal to producer; our transfers run buyer to seller. The signs, global IC proof, exclusion qualifications and exact bunching certificate above have been derived for this chapter’s value-type model.

2. Continuum IC without a differentiability assumption

Let θ range over a compact interval [a,b], a<b. A deterministic direct menu assigns a bounded quality q(θ)∈[0,Q] and a finite payment t(θ). Put U(θ)=θq(θ)−t(θ). IC compares every pair of reports, including endpoints and points with zero probability under the distribution.

Envelope characterization. The menu is IC if and only if q is nondecreasing and, for some finite U(a),

U(θ)=U(a)+∫aθq(s)ds,   t(θ)=θq(θ)−U(θ).

Necessity, including jumps. The same two IC inequalities as in the finite case imply, for x<y,

(y−x)q(x)≤U(y)−U(x)≤(y−x)q(y).

Hence q is nondecreasing and |U(y)−U(x)|≤Q|y−x|. On any partition a=x0<⋯<xm=θ, sum these bounds to sandwich U(θ)−U(a) between the lower and upper sums for q. Their difference is at most maxk(xk−xk−1)Σk[q(xk)−q(xk−1)]≤Q times the mesh. As the mesh tends to zero, both sums converge to the same Riemann integral. This proves the formula without assuming that the chosen menu or U is differentiable. In particular, U is continuous and absolutely continuous; its derivative equals q almost everywhere, but need not exist at a jump of q.

Sufficiency. If q is nondecreasing and bounded, then for x<y its integral on [x,y] lies between (y−x)q(x) and (y−x)q(y). Substituting U(y)−U(x) gives both cross-report IC inequalities. They hold for every pair, including a jump point whose chosen quality lies between its left and right limits. Since q≥0, U is nondecreasing; IR for every type is equivalent to U(a)≥0. For a fixed quality function, IC therefore fixes all rents and payments up to the one constant U(a). This differs from the finite case, where an adjacent utility increment can lie anywhere in an interval.

For expected profit, assume the distribution has a continuous strictly positive density f on [a,b], normalized to integrate to one, and let F(θ)=∫aθf(s)ds. Assume c is continuous and convex on [0,Q]. All allocations and costs are bounded, and monotone q is measurable. The nonnegative bounded rent integral permits changing the order of integration; equivalently, integrate over the triangle a≤s≤θ≤b:

E[U]=U(a)+∫abq(s)[1−F(s)]ds,
Π=∫abf(θ)[φ(θ)q(θ)−c(q(θ))]dθ−U(a),
φ(θ)=θ−[1−F(θ)]/f(θ).

Strict positivity and continuity of f on the compact interval keep this displayed ratio well-defined and bounded. It is not an instruction to divide by zero in an empirical or irregular distribution. The seller chooses U(a)=0. If the pointwise maximizing allocation for φ(θ)q−c(q) on [0,Q] is nondecreasing, it is globally optimal among IC allocations: integrate its pointwise inequality against positive f. If that allocation is not monotone, the pointwise answer is infeasible; a constrained argument is needed, as the finite bunching case illustrated. We do not supply a general continuum ironing algorithm here.

Worked case 3: a continuum with an endogenous exclusion threshold

Take θ uniform on [1,3], Q=5, with c(q)=q²/2. Here f=1/2 and 1−F(θ)=(3−θ)/2, so φ(θ)=2θ−3. Completing the square gives the feasible, nondecreasing allocation

q*(θ)=max(0,2θ−3),
U*(θ)=0 if θ≤3/2, and (θ−3/2)² if θ≥3/2,
t*(θ)=0 if θ≤3/2, and θ²−9/4 if θ≥3/2.

The formulas agree at the threshold. Quality never exceeds three, so the cap is slack. Every below-threshold type obtains the outside contract; above it, envelope rent grows with type. For θ=2 the triple (q,U,t) is (1,1/4,7/4); at θ=3 it is (3,9/4,27/4). The pointwise maximization and the envelope construction prove global IC/IR and global profit optimality together. Strict concavity gives uniqueness of q only almost everywhere under the density. Our displayed formula selects a continuous representative. For example, the top endpoint alone could instead receive q(3)∈[3,5] with t(3)=3q(3)−9/4 while preserving IC and expected profit; it has probability zero. This is why an almost-everywhere claim must not be silently upgraded to pointwise uniqueness.

All expectations can be recomputed from the primitives:

E[t]=(1/2)∫3/23(θ²−9/4)dθ=9/4,
E[c]=(1/2)∫3/23(2θ−3)²/2 dθ=9/8,
Π=9/8,   E[U]=(1/2)∫3/23(θ−3/2)²dθ=9/16.

Total surplus is 27/16. The feasible full-information allocation q=θ gives (1/2)∫13θ²/2 dθ=13/6, leaving a loss of 23/48. The information-rent term lowers supplied quality; a rent payment itself is a transfer and is not additionally subtracted from total surplus.

Holmström’s slides 24–35 motivate the envelope and virtual-cost transformation. The slides expressly assume differentiability for their derivation. Our pairwise/Riemann proof supplies the nonsmooth result needed for the step-allocation exercise, with the payment direction translated throughout.

3. Random contracts: exactly when taking means is valid

Allow a report r to select a lottery (qr,tr), with qr∈[0,Q] almost surely and E|tr|<∞. Buyer and seller are risk neutral in money, and buyer value is still linear in quality. The buyer knows its type and chooses whether to participate and which report to make before the lottery is drawn. The contract is enforceable after the draw; there is no later rejection or renegotiation right. Interim utility means expectation over that contract lottery, conditional on the buyer’s known type.

For a continuum of reports, also require the lottery family to have jointly measurable quality and payment realizations on the type/report interval and a common probability space, and require ∫abE[|tθ|]f(θ)dθ<∞. Per-report integrability alone does not ensure that ex ante receipts exist. This additional condition makes aggregate payments absolutely integrable; bounded quality and continuous cost already make aggregate production cost finite. In the finite-type case, finitely many integrable report payments supply this aggregate condition automatically.

Mean-contract theorem. If production cost is continuous and convex on [0,Q], replacing every report lottery by the deterministic pair (E[qr],E[tr]) preserves every type’s interim utility from every report and weakly raises seller profit. Consequently any feasible randomized menu in this class has a deterministic menu with the same interim IC/IR and at least as much profit.

Proof. For any θ and report r, E[θqr−tr]=θE[qr]−E[tr]. Thus all the comparisons defining interim IC and participation are identical after replacement, including ties. Mean quality remains in [0,Q]. Jensen’s inequality gives c(E[qr])≤E[c(qr)], while expected payment is unchanged. Summing by type, or integrating the measurable inequalities under the stated aggregate integrability condition, proves the profit claim with finite expected receipts and costs. For completeness, a continuous convex c has a supporting line at an interior mean m: convex secant slopes to the left are no larger than those to the right, so a slope α between their limiting bounds satisfies c(q)≥c(m)+α(q−m) on [0,Q]. Expectations give Jensen. If m=0 or Q, bounded q must equal that endpoint almost surely, so equality holds. This also covers non-finite lotteries without assuming differentiability of c.

Strictly convex cost makes the cost inequality strict for a nonconstant quality lottery, but random payments alone need not cost anything under the maintained risk neutrality. With risk aversion, nonlinear utility from quality, correlated private risks, ex-post rejection, or different contractual restrictions, replacing a lottery by its means need not preserve utility or feasibility. Those are changes to the model, not exceptions to its proof.

Worked case 4: convexity and the date of participation

For types θ=(2,4), quality q=(0,4) with probabilities (1/2,1/2), fixed payment t=3, the mean contract is quality two at payment three. Either committed contract gives interim utilities (1,5). Under c(q)=q²/2, deterministic cost is two but expected lottery cost is four. The respective seller profits are (1,−1). This is a statement about each participating type, so no type prior is needed for the comparison.

Now change only technology to c(q)=√q, which is concave, not convex. Deterministic profit is 3−√2, whereas lottery profit is 2; the latter is larger because √2>1. Utility from every report is still preserved, but the convex-cost inequality has reversed in this example. We have compared two fixed contracts, not solved the globally optimal randomized menu under a new technology.

At the zero-quality realization the buyer’s utility is −3 for either type, despite positive interim expected utility. Thus interim IR is not ex-post IR. Giving the buyer a free option to reject after seeing quality would change both expected payment and incentives; one cannot reuse the committed-contract numbers while adding that right.

4. A complete pure signaling equilibrium correspondence

Nature chooses type L or H with productivities (vL,vH)=(2,5) and Pr(H)=1/3. The worker observes its own type, chooses education s≥0, and employers observe s but not type. Education initially changes no productivity. Its utility costs are cL(s)=s and cH(s)=s/3. These costs are real disutility in our welfare calculation, not transfers to another modeled agent.

Pricing is a maintained condition. A posterior μ(s)=Pr(H|s) determines wage w(s)=2+3μ(s). We impose this posterior-mean competitive wage formula. We have not specified a separate wage-bidding game and proved that competition produces it. The admissible wage at every signal lies in [2,5]. Workers maximize w(s)−cθ(s) over all s≥0.

A pure PBE assessment in this pricing model consists of signals sL,sH, a posterior μ(s)∈[0,1] at every signal, and the prescribed wage w(s), such that each type’s chosen signal is a global best response and μ satisfies Bayes’ rule at every positive-probability on-path signal. If the signals differ, μ(sL)=0 and μ(sH)=1. If they coincide at sp, μ(sp)=1/3. Off-path beliefs are unrestricted by Bayes alone. A type may choose any of its utility-maximizing signals, including at indifference. This is a complete definition for the present model; we do not infer it from finite sequential-equilibrium existence.

Single crossing orders pure signals. Add the inequalities stating that L prefers sL to sH and H prefers sH to sL. Wages cancel, leaving (1−1/3)(sH−sL)≥0. Hence sH≥sL. With two types a pure profile is either pooling or separating; there is no additional pure category.

Worked case 5: all pure equilibria before and after a belief refinement

Every separating outcome. If the signals differ, H chooses more education. The low type receives wage two. If sL>0, deviating to zero gives a wage at least two and avoids a positive cost; that is strictly better. Therefore sL=0. Write sH=h>0. Low’s non-mimicry and high’s participation at the low signal require

2≥5−h,   5−h/3≥2.

Thus all possible separating education pairs are (0,h), h∈[3,9]. These necessary conditions are sufficient. Set μ(0)=0, μ(h)=1 and μ(s)=0 at every other signal. Then any off-path deviation gives L at most two and H at most two, while their equilibrium utilities are two and 5−h/3≥2. The cross-signal inequalities cover the remaining deviations. This constructs a complete wage schedule and proves existence for every h in the interval, including both equality endpoints.

Every pooling outcome. Bayes gives wage three at a common signal sp. If sp>0, low can deviate to zero and obtain at least two, so 3−sp≥2. Conversely, for any sp∈[0,1], choose μ(sp)=1/3 and low beliefs elsewhere. Low’s payoff is at least two; high’s is 3−sp/3≥2. All off-path payoffs are at most two. This includes zero pooling, where zero is on path rather than a distinct deviation. Hence the interval is exact. Bayes and best responses alone do not select the least costly separating signal.

The refinement must be stated before using it. Let U*θ be a type’s equilibrium payoff and consider an off-path signal s. Its equilibrium-dominated type set is

D(s)={θ:U*θ>maxμ∈[0,1][2+3μ−cθ(s)]}
={θ:U*θ>5−cθ(s)}.

The comparison is strict: a type that could only tie its equilibrium payoff is not in D(s). We use the belief formulation of the Intuitive Criterion specialized to our maintained competitive response set. If D(s) is nonempty and is not the whole type set, the posterior must give its members zero probability. If D(s) is empty, no type is excluded; if every type is dominated, there is no additional restriction. A PBE whose required posterior then gives a type a strictly profitable deviation cannot survive. Our refinements below all force the singleton H posterior, so this also supplies the strict profitable-deviation test after eliminating dominated types.

Eliminate every pooling outcome. At sp∈[0,1], payoffs are 3−sp for L and 3−sp/3 for H. Choose any off-path signal

s∈(2+sp,6+sp).

The interval is nonempty and lies above the pooling signal. Low’s best possible deviation payoff 5−s is strictly below 3−sp, whereas high’s 5−s/3 is strictly above 3−sp/3. Thus D(s)={L}; the criterion requires μ(s)=1. The resulting wage five makes H strictly prefer the deviation, contradicting equilibrium. This rules out every member of the pooling interval, not just a sampled signal.

Eliminate every separating outcome with h>3. Choose s∈(3,h). Low’s equilibrium payoff two strictly exceeds 5−s. High’s maximal deviation payoff 5−s/3 strictly exceeds 5−h/3. Again the criterion forces H belief and a strict H deviation. The intervals remain nonempty when h is arbitrarily close to three.

Construct survival at h=3. At the pair (0,3), payoffs are (2,4). For any off-path 0<s<3, both types could strictly gain at maximal wage five, so neither is dominated. Choose low belief: low obtains 2−s<2 and high obtains 2−s/3<4. For s>3, both maximal payoffs are strictly below their respective equilibrium payoffs, so every type is dominated and the criterion imposes no restriction. Low belief again deters. Signals zero and three already have the Bayes-consistent beliefs. At s=3 low is indifferent between imitation and its own signal; allowing its chosen best response is essential.

We have proved a unique surviving pure education outcome, (0,3). Off-path beliefs are not unique. We have neither classified mixed signaling strategies nor proved uniqueness across all mixed/hybrid outcomes. This conclusion resolves the introductory selection question only in the explicit scope just proved.

Selection and welfare differ. Average productivity is three regardless of education. In the surviving separation, high types incur cost one and have probability one third, so expected net welfare is 8/3. Pooling at zero would give welfare three but fails this refinement. Wage transfers do not create productivity; because wages equal conditional expected output, expected employer profit is zero and expected worker utility equals output minus education cost. A refinement is an incentive/belief restriction, not a social-planner objective.

Manea’s notes, pages 54–61 supply the inspected strict equilibrium-dominance and signaling refinement architecture. The formal test at pages 54–55 ranges over rational responses to surviving types; the belief formulation and all-dominated exception appear on page 60. Our wage interval is a maintained competitive response set, and all constants, pure classifications and survival constructions above are proved for our own primitives. Claims about hybrid uniqueness in the source are outside this chapter’s proof scope.

5. Productive education and the failure of strict selection at a boundary

Change productivity to vθ+κs, while retaining the two original private education costs and prior. Education’s productive contribution is the same for both types and is observed through s. The maintained wage becomes w(s)=2+3μ(s)+κs. Worker net utility can be written 2+3μ(s)−aθs, where

aL=1−κ,   aH=1/3−κ.

The difference aL−aH=2/3 remains positive, but the sign of each net cost matters. Treating κ as “just another positive productivity number” would miss a qualitative equilibrium boundary.

Positive net costs: 0≤κ<1/3. The single-crossing order proof still applies. In separation, aL>0 makes any positive low signal strictly worse than deviating to zero, so sL=0. The two cross-signal constraints are 2≥5−aLh and 5−aHh≥2. Hence every pure separating outcome and every pure pooling outcome are respectively

(0,h),   3/aL≤h≤3/aH;   sp∈[0,1/aL].

For pooling, the posterior base wage is three, so low’s comparison with zero gives 3−aLsp≥2. Since 0<aH<aL, this also ensures high’s payoff is at least two. Low beliefs at all off-path signals yield payoffs 2−aθs≤2 and prove sufficiency for both families. Necessity and these complete belief constructions classify all pure outcomes.

At any off-path s the maximal payoff is now 5−aθs. For pooling choose s∈(sp+2/aL,sp+2/aH). Low is strictly dominated and high strictly benefits under H belief. For separation with h>3/aL, choose s∈(3/aL,h); the same strict comparisons apply. At the least-cost h0=3/aL, every off-path 0<s<h0 leaves both types undominated, and every s>h0 makes both dominated. Low off-path beliefs deter all deviations exactly as before. Thus h0 is again the unique surviving pure separating education level, without asserting uniqueness of beliefs or mixed outcomes.

Worked case 6: a productive signal, then the zero-net-cost boundary

Take κ=1/6. Net costs are (5/6,1/6); the separating interval is [18/5,18] and the pooling interval is [0,6/5]. Refinement selects high education 18/5. High wage is 28/5 and high net utility is 22/5; the low type earns two. Expected output is 16/5, expected education cost is 2/5, and net welfare is 14/5. These numbers distinguish the wage premium, the productive increment and the remaining signaling cost.

At κ=1/3, strict selection fails. Now aL=2/3 but aH=0. All pure separating outcomes have sL=0 and h≥9/2. Low non-mimicry gives this lower bound, while high earns base payoff five at every H-priced signal, independently of its education. The high type’s comparison with the low signal is always 5≥2. Basic PBE support follows from low off-path beliefs, but those beliefs need adjustment to satisfy the criterion.

Fix any finite h≥9/2. At any off-path s>9/2, low’s maximal payoff 5−(2/3)s is strictly below its equilibrium payoff two. High’s maximal payoff is five, exactly its equilibrium payoff: high is not equilibrium dominated. Therefore the criterion requires H belief at every off-path s>9/2. The resulting high payoff is still five, so there is no strict gain; low receives strictly less than two. At 0<s<9/2 neither type is dominated; assign low belief, yielding low payoff at most two and high payoff two. If s=9/2 is off path because h>9/2, low’s maximal payoff merely ties two, so neither type is dominated; low belief is permitted there too. Retain Bayes beliefs at zero and h. This full assessment supports every finite h≥9/2 and respects the refinement, including equality cases. Calling high’s zero gain a strict gain would incorrectly select a unique signal.

For completeness, basic pooling outcomes at this boundary are sp∈[0,3/2]. Choose any s>sp+3: low is strictly dominated while high can obtain five instead of three, so refinement still eliminates pooling. The surviving pure set is precisely the separating half-line, with the belief restrictions just established. Every such separation has net welfare three: productive increment h/9 and expected cost h/9 offset. Equal welfare does not itself prove survival; the incentive and belief construction does.

For κ>1/3 no finite high-type best response exists. Whatever beliefs are assigned, the wage is at least 2+κs, so high’s payoff is at least 2+(κ−1/3)s. This lower bound tends to infinity. Every finite signal has a finite wage and utility and is beaten by a sufficiently large signal. Thus no pure PBE with a finite high action exists in this unbounded-signal model. A cap, convexly rising private cost or a different productive technology would be a new model requiring new analysis; equilibrium cannot be rescued by choosing pessimistic beliefs alone.

6. Solving and interpreting an information problem

Begin by identifying what is privately known, when it is known, what can be contracted on, and who commits. Then write every available deviation and the date at which participation is evaluated. A direct menu is useful only if its reported contracts are enforceable; a signaling wage is meaningful only with a specified pricing response and information set.

For finite screening, first test monotonicity and adjacent utility bounds, then verify all pairs as a diagnostic. Set rents minimally only after showing that the resulting menu stays IC/IR. Optimize the virtual objective on its entire constrained domain, including quality zero, caps and bunching. For a continuum, derive the envelope and integration conditions before using a pointwise formula. For signaling, derive necessary outcome restrictions and then construct beliefs at every off-path signal to prove sufficiency. A chosen deviation can refute equilibrium; checking a few deviations cannot prove global best response.

The theory does not identify private types from a fitted menu or prove that observed education has a causal wage effect. Type-dependent costs, productive education, selection into employment, borrowing limits and contract enforcement can produce different interpretations. To connect a model to evidence, specify observed data, unobserved heterogeneity, feasible policy variation and the counterfactual information regime. A belief refinement narrows predictions under maintained assumptions; it is not observed employer behavior.

Reproduction. The finite cases can be reconstructed using exact rational arithmetic: calculate each Ui and ti, build all n² IC gaps, aggregate expected payment and cost, and verify the tangent bound. The continuum cases require only integration of the displayed polynomials. For signaling, test the stated endpoint inequalities and the complete piecewise belief construction, retaining strict versus weak signs. Editorial checks additionally enumerate bounded finite active sets and classify the exact linear deviation regions; they supplement the proofs and do not turn a numerical grid into an existence or uniqueness theorem.

7. Exercises

Use exact fractions unless a question explicitly calls for qualitative evaluation. All menus retain commitment and the stated truth/participation tie convention; all signaling questions retain the maintained posterior-mean wage formula and allow an indicated utility-maximizing signal at indifference.

  1. A prior change and additional exclusion. Keep the types, quadratic cost and cap from worked case 1, but replace the probabilities by (1/4,1/4,1/2). Derive the globally optimal menu, not just an unconstrained first-order condition. Check IC/IR, calculate profit, observable-type first-best surplus and the surplus loss. Identify which types have zero rent.
  2. Bunching with a binding cap. In worked case 2 reduce only the common quality cap to Q=1. Find all three qualities, rents and payments and expected profit. Give a global tangent certificate that covers both the monotonicity and cap constraints; prove uniqueness of the allocation.
  3. Strict reporting and weak participation. At the qualities of worked case 1, consider the alternative utility list U=(0,1/2,5/2). Construct the payments and all off-diagonal IC gaps. Is truthful reporting strict? Is participation strict? Calculate seller profit and compare it with the minimal-rent optimum. Explain what adding the same δ>0 to all three utilities does to IC, IR and expected profit.
  4. A jump and the derivative trap. On θ∈[1,3], set q(θ)=0 for θ<2; q(θ)=2 for θ>2; q(2)=a∈[0,2]. With U(1)=0, construct U and t and prove global IC for every permitted a, including the type θ=2. Explain why writing U′(2)=q(2) is unjustified. Under the uniform distribution and quadratic cost, calculate expected payment, cost and profit.
  5. A different continuum. Let θ be uniform on [1,4], Q=5, with quadratic cost q²/2. Derive a continuous representative of the optimal menu and its exclusion threshold. Calculate expected payment, cost, profit, rent, total surplus, first-best surplus and the loss. State the exact uniqueness qualification.
  6. A later rejection right. For types 2 and 4, offer quality 0 with probability 1/3 and quality 3 with probability 2/3, with payment 3. First calculate committed interim utilities and quadratic-cost profit and compare with the mean contract. Then add a right to reject after quality is revealed, paying nothing and receiving zero quality if rejected; production cost is incurred only for accepted quality. Determine each type’s decision at each realization, expected utilities, payment, cost and profit. Explain why one cannot retain the first calculation after adding this right.
  7. A belief prior changes pooling. In worked case 5 change only the high prior to Pr(H)=1/2. Characterize all pure pooling and separating education outcomes with supporting beliefs. Prove which survive the same criterion. Calculate welfare in least-cost separation and in zero-education pooling.
  8. Strict dominance is type specific. Under the original signaling primitives, examine the off-path signal s=4 separately at pooling sp=1, separation h=6, and least-cost separation h=3. For each, calculate equilibrium payoffs, maximal deviation payoffs, D(4), the resulting belief restriction and whether this signal refutes the equilibrium. Do not treat “all types dominated” as a requirement to remove every type from the posterior.
  9. Productive education transfer. Set κ=1/4. Derive the exact pure pooling and separating intervals and the surviving pure outcome. Calculate its high wage, high net utility, average output, education cost and net welfare. Explain why these model quantities do not identify a causal education effect from observational wages.
  10. The equality boundary and nonexistence beyond it. At κ=1/3 and separating h=6, determine the criterion’s restrictions at off-path signals five and four. Supply a complete refined-PBE belief schedule and calculate high’s deviation payoff at five. Then change κ to 1/2 and prove that no finite high-type best response exists for any posterior schedule. A finite numerical search is not an acceptable proof.
  11. Research critique. A report observes increasing posted quality and payment, and a positive association between education and wages. It claims these observations establish the optimal screening menu, show that education is unproductive, and validate the unique equilibrium of the labor market. Write a concise referee assessment separating the maintained models, what the observations show, what is unidentified, and one feasible design for additional evidence. Address commitment, participation timing and the scope of the refinement. Use the solution rubric rather than accepting any particular policy preference.
  12. Fixed quality does not mean arbitrary rents. Hold the entire continuous quality function of worked case 3 fixed, including endpoints, but set U(1)=δ. Characterize every IC payment function at that quality, its IR domain and profit. Evaluate δ=1/4 and explain why the seller chooses δ=0. Contrast this one-dimensional freedom with the finite utility list in exercise 3; prove the contrast from the relevant IC characterizations.
Complete solutions, proof checks and critique rubric

  1. The new virtual values are (−2,0,3). Each quadratic scalar objective is maximized at its clipped virtual value, giving the already monotone q=(0,0,3). This is a global optimum by the same pointwise bound, and strict concavity with positive probabilities gives a unique quality vector. Minimal rents are (0,0,0), and payments are (0,0,9). Each type can obtain zero through exclusion; types one and two obtain negative utility from the top contract, while type three is indifferent. The lower two contracts coincide, so all IC/IR hold with the declared tie convention. Profit is (1/2)(9−9/2)=9/4, and zero rent makes this also total surplus. Observable-type surplus is (1/4)(1/2)+(1/4)(2)+(1/2)(9/2)=23/8, so the loss is 5/8. Every type has zero rent; the high type’s zero rent is compatible with positive supplied quality because all lower qualities are zero.

  2. The solution is q*=(2/3,2/3,1). Minimal rents stay (0,2/3,4/3), because they depend on lower qualities, and payments become (4/3,4/3,8/3). Monotonicity and the minimal-rent construction prove all IC/IR. Expected profit is (3/5)(4/3−2/9)+(2/5)(8/3−1/2)=23/15. The virtual-objective gradient is (1/6,−1/6,6/5). For every feasible q, the tangent gain is (q1−q2)/6+(6/5)(q3−1)≤0. Subtracting the strictly positive weighted quadratic remainder gives Π(q)≤Π(q*), with equality only at q*. The positive third gradient is consistent with an optimum because the cap binds; setting every gradient equal to zero would be incorrect.

  3. Payments are (0,3/2,13/2). Listing the off-diagonal gaps row by row in report order gives (1/2,7/2; 1/2,1; 5/2,1), all strictly positive. Thus truth is strictly preferred to every other report, while the lowest type still has utility zero and is indifferent to not participating. Profit is (1/4)(3/2−1/2)+(1/4)(13/2−9/2)=3/4, lower than the worked optimum by 1/2. The alternative allocates unnecessary information rent without changing quality. Adding δ to every U lowers every payment by δ. Every report’s utility rises by δ for every true type, leaving all IC gaps unchanged. IR becomes strict, and normalized type probabilities make expected profit decrease by exactly δ. Transfers were allowed to be negative, so the lowest contract’s resulting rebate is feasible in this model.

  4. The integral formula gives U(θ)=2 max(θ−2,0). Payments are zero below two, t(2)=2a at two, and four above two. Monotonicity holds for a∈[0,2], so the envelope sufficiency theorem proves global IC. Explicitly, a below-threshold type gets nonpositive utility from any positive-quality offer; an above-threshold type gets at most its own 2(θ−2) from the intermediate offer a; and type two obtains zero from every offered contract. This also checks the equality point that has zero probability under the uniform law. U has left derivative zero and right derivative two at θ=2, so its ordinary derivative there does not exist, regardless of the selected a. The singleton does not affect expectations: expected payment is 2, cost is 1, and profit is 1. The envelope is an integral statement, not a requirement that U be differentiable at every type.

  5. Density is 1/3, tail probability (4−θ)/3, and virtual value 2θ−4. The scalar quadratic optimum is q=max(0,2θ−4), continuous and nondecreasing with maximum four below the cap. With U(1)=0, both rent and payment vanish for θ≤2; above two, U=(θ−2)² and t=θ²−4. Hence the threshold is 2. Exact integration over [2,4] with density 1/3 gives (E[t],E[c],Π,E[U])=(32/9,16/9,16/9,8/9). Total surplus is 8/3. First best q=θ is feasible and gives (4³−1)/(6·3)=7/2, so the loss is 5/6. Pointwise bounds prove global profit optimality. Strict concavity gives uniqueness almost everywhere, and the displayed continuous representative chooses its endpoint qualities; IC alone can permit null-set endpoint differences without altering expected profit.

  6. Mean quality is two. With commitment, interim utilities are (1,5); expected production cost is (2/3)(9/2)=3, so seller profit is 0. The deterministic mean contract has cost two and profit one. With the later rejection right, both types strictly reject zero quality because accepting would give −3; both strictly accept quality three because utilities are three and nine. Their new expected utilities are (2,6). Expected payment, cost and seller profit become (2,3,−1). No cost is incurred for the rejected zero-quality outcome. The right is valuable to the buyer and removes a payment in that realization, so the original committed calculation is no longer its contract. This does not contradict the theorem: the theorem held fixed the participation date and enforceable lottery payment.

  7. The pooling wage is 7/2. Low’s zero-signal comparison gives pooling sp∈[0,3/2]; high’s condition is weaker. Low beliefs at every off-path signal support all these poolings. Separating on-path posteriors remain zero and one because both prior probabilities are positive, so the same arguments give h∈[3,9] with sL=0 and low off-path support. Every pooling fails refinement: choose s∈(sp+3/2,sp+9/2), which strictly dominates L’s deviation incentive while giving H a strict gain at wage five. Excess separating h>3 is eliminated by the unchanged interval (3,h), and the same belief construction supports h=3. Average productivity is 7/2, and half the workers incur education cost one in least-cost separation, so welfare is 3. Zero-education pooling has welfare 7/2. A change in the prior affects pooling wages and aggregate welfare even when the separating signal constraints do not change.

  8. At signal four, maximal deviation payoffs (L,H) are always (1,11/3). Pooling at one gives (2,8/3); therefore D(4)={L}, H belief is forced, and H strictly gains. Separation at six gives (2,3); again D(4)={L}, and the forced deviation improves H by 2/3. Least-cost separation gives (2,4), both strictly larger than the maximal deviation payoffs, so D(4)={L,H}. The criterion then imposes no restriction, and even wage five cannot make either type prefer this signal. It would be a logical error to demand a posterior with zero mass on both types. The full survival proof still requires the other signals, already supplied in worked case 5.

  9. Net costs are (3/4,1/12), both positive. All pure separations have h in [4,36], and all pure poolings have sp in [0,4/3]. The general open-interval deviations remove pooling and all h>4, and the full least-cost belief construction admits (0,4). High wage is 6, high net utility 14/3. Average output is 10/3, expected education cost 4/9, and net welfare 26/9. These are implications of the stipulated κ and cost/prior structure. Observational wages combine productive effects, private selection and posterior responses; they do not by themselves identify κ, the cost difference or what beliefs would do under a policy change.

  10. Equilibrium payoffs at h=6 are (2,5). At s=5, maximal payoffs are (5/3,5), so D(5)={L}. H belief is required, giving wage 20/3 and high utility five after paying education cost 5/3. High ties, and there is no profitable deviation. At s=4, maximal payoffs are (7/3,5); neither type is dominated. Choose low belief there, giving high utility two and low utility −2/3. A complete schedule sets μ(0)=0, μ(6)=1, μ(s)=1 at every other s>9/2, and μ(s)=0 at all remaining signals. Below or at 9/2 off path no extra restriction binds, above it only low is dominated, and every resulting payoff is at most its equilibrium value. This proves a refined pure assessment globally. If κ=1/2 instead, high’s payoff at s is at least 2+s/6, whatever μ(s). Given any finite current utility u, choose s>max(0,6(u−2)); the lower bound then exceeds u. Every finite signal is beaten, proving nonexistence of a finite high best response without a grid or local condition.

  11. Evaluation rubric. A satisfactory assessment covers four linked points. First, distinguish the observations from structural claims: rising posted qualities/prices alone do not reveal types, actual choices, cost curvature or whether any global IC/IR optimum is being implemented. Discuss menu commitment, enforceable quality and selection among ties. Second, explain that risk neutrality, interim participation and no later rejection are maintained contract assumptions; observed prices cannot establish them, and exercise 6 shows why changing a right changes cash and utility. Third, a wage/education association cannot establish zero productive return or the assumed type-dependent cost; nor can it reveal all off-path beliefs. Our theorem selects only pure outcomes under an explicitly imposed criterion, with a counterexample to unique selection at the productive boundary. Fourth, propose evidence with a credible information/timing design: for example, randomize feasible menu offers under fixed audited enforcement and measure actual uptake, quality and costs, while separately studying a plausibly exogenous education opportunity and its employment/production consequences. State compliance, selection, spillover and external-validity limitations; merely comparing selected participants is insufficient.

    An excellent answer specifies which parameter or model restriction each new observation tests and which remain unidentified, considers an alternative explanation such as financing constraints or cost heterogeneity, and distinguishes a falsifiable implication from an assumed equilibrium selection. No particular intervention or welfare ranking is required. A response that repeats the report’s causal or universal uniqueness claims fails even if it fits the displayed numerical cases.

  12. By necessity of the continuum envelope, every IC utility at this fixed q equals the worked U*(θ)+δ. Thus every payment is t*(θ)−δ; sufficiency proves all these menus are IC. Since the minimum rent occurs at θ=1 and equals δ, IR for every type holds exactly when δ≥0. Profit is 9/8−δ, so at δ=1/4 it is 7/8. The seller chooses δ=0 because a positive common utility shift costs exactly that amount without changing quality or report comparisons. In the finite case, each adjacent rent difference may range between Δθiqi and Δθiqi+1; exercise 3 takes interior values and raises the two gaps by different amounts. In the continuum, finer partitions force the lower/upper sums to coincide, removing these independent gaps. The contrast follows from the two proved characterizations, not from assuming smoothness or unique reporting.

8. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain to a colleague why a seller can optimally exclude a low-value buyer, why two different types may receive one contract, and why a signaling refinement need not improve welfare. A complete explanation identifies the rent imposed on higher types by raising lower quality; shows how monotonicity can constrain otherwise distinct pointwise optima; and distinguishes posterior credibility from aggregate output minus real cost. Use the exclusion and bunching certificates rather than the slogan “information causes inefficiency.” The zero-education pool and refined separation provide the welfare counterexample.

Delayed retention, without the formulas. Reconstruct the finite adjacent IC bounds, then explain why they telescope. State what happens to the continuum envelope at a quality jump. Explain why taking lottery means requires a fixed participation date. Finally, decide whether high’s indifference at κ=1/3 makes high equilibrium dominated.

Answer key. The lower bound is the type gap times lower quality, and the upper bound is the gap times higher quality; monotonicity bounds the sums by the endpoint qualities and gives every global IC comparison. The integral envelope remains valid at a jump although an ordinary derivative need not exist there. Moving acceptance after the draw changes the payoff from bad realizations, so the old report utilities and cash receipts need not be preserved. Equilibrium dominance requires a strict loss even under the best admissible response; equality does not qualify. At the zero-net-cost boundary the criterion therefore forces H beliefs above the low deterrence threshold while H remains indifferent.

The next chapter, Contracts and dynamic incentives, turns from private types to hidden action, limited liability and limited commitment. Before reusing today’s menu reasoning, identify whether the agent can change an unobserved action after signing and whether promised future transfers remain credible. Those additions create new incentive constraints rather than merely a longer type list.
